content:
Chief Executive John Lee visited the district this afternoon, accompanied by Secretary for Health Professor Lo Chung-mau and Secretary for Youth and Civic Affairs Alice Mak. He first paid a home visit to an elderly resident surnamed Chan who had recently been discharged from hospital after pneumonia treatment. The 88-year-old said the day-time medical centre made it convenient for her to get follow-up chest X-rays, easing the burden on family members who accompany her to appointments.

Residents shout 'John Lee is so handsome'

He then visited the Baptist Elderly Centre in the estate and tried out a smart exercise bike in the estate park. Before leaving, he posed for photos and chatted with residents, some of whom shouted 'John Lee is so handsome' and 'I support you'. He later toured the operations of the government's 1823 hotline.

To publish five-year plan and Policy Address on the same day, September 16

Speaking to the media afterwards alongside Secretary Mak and Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong, Lee said the purpose of today's district visit was to understand how policies in the Policy Address were being implemented on the ground. He said hearing the views of many elderly residents would help shape the five-year plan and the Policy Address. He announced that Hong Kong's first five-year plan and the Policy Address would both be released on September 16, so the public could see how the two were closely linked.

He explained that the Policy Address is the Chief Executive's annual report on implementing the five-year plan. 'To put it simply,' Lee said, 'the five-year plan dots the eyes of the dragon, and the Policy Address redraws the dragon each year.' Releasing both documents at the same time would help the public understand how the two are connected.

Responding to dog-on-dog and dog-on-person attacks: 'Hope dog owners take responsibility'

Following a recent spate of incidents involving dogs attacking other dogs and people, Lee said the cases had attracted public concern and showed how important owner responsibility was. Dogs needed to be properly controlled, and he hoped owners would take their responsibilities seriously. Anyone who irresponsibly broke the law must be dealt with in accordance with the law. As for dog attacks on people, the Environment and Ecology Bureau and the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department would review penalties and whether the definition of fighting dogs needed to be revisited. He added that public education was also important, and he hoped every dog owner would take responsibility.

Hongkong Post losses: 'I believe reform is necessary'

Responding to questions about Hongkong Post's operations, Lee said the issues it faced were unique. Hongkong Post operates on a commercial, self-financing model, and the postal ecosystem has changed dramatically, partly due to digitalisation. The operating environment is very different from before, with losses of HK$800 million in 2024-25 and a recent application to the Legislative Council for more than HK$4 billion in operating funding over three years. 'I believe reform of Hongkong Post is necessary,' he said, adding that the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau would examine the matter and put forward proposals as soon as possible.

CE and three Secretaries plus Security chief publish articles on 'Coordinating development and security'

Lee recently published an article titled 'Coordinating development and security', in which he wrote: 'Hong Kong has moved from chaos to order, and is now moving from order to prosperity. Coordinating development and security is therefore more important than ever.' He said: 'Security is the prerequisite for development, and development is the guarantee of security. The two have always been mutually reinforcing — coexisting rather than opposed.' On the same day, Chief Secretary Eric Chan, Financial Secretary Paul Chan, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam and Secretary for Security Chris Tang also published commentaries on related topics.

Eric Chan said: 'How to balance security and development — giving both equal weight so they support and reinforce each other — is the key to ensuring the steady and far-reaching implementation of "One Country, Two Systems".' Paul Chan said: 'Hong Kong's current positive development momentum is premised on coordinating development and security, allowing the two to reinforce each other.' Paul Lam described it as 'the most authoritative legal articulation of the inseparable and closely linked relationship between security and development.' Chris Tang said: 'Security and development are like the two wheels of a cart and the two wings of a bird. They reinforce each other and neither can be dispensed with.'
